title: De and het — two kinds of nouns
goal: Recognize how Dutch nouns split into de-woorden and het-woorden, use *een*, and form plurals with *-en* or *-s*.
bekal: know why *de* and *het* can't be guessed — and which groups can
form plurals: *het boek → de boeken*, *de tafel → de tafels*
use the small form *-je*, which turns every word into a het-woord
wave: Review **Unit 1**: cover the Dutch column of the greetings table, look at the times, and say each greeting from memory, out loud.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — In de klas
dialogs.intro: The teacher points at things around the classroom. Budi starts to suspect something is off with Dutch articles.

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: Dit is een tafel. De tafel is bruin.
lines.id: This is a table. The table is brown.
lines.literal: this is a table. the table is brown.

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: En dit is een boek. Het boek is nieuw.
lines.id: And this is a book. The book is new.
lines.literal: and this is a book. the book is new.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Waarom de tafel, maar het boek?
lines.id: Why de tafel, but het boek?
lines.literal: why the table, but the book?

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: Goede vraag. Daar is geen regel voor.
lines.id: Good question. There's no rule for it.
lines.literal: good question. there is no rule for.

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: Bijna niet. Je leert het woord met de of het samen.
lines.id: Almost none. You learn the word together with its de or het.
lines.literal: almost not. you learn the word with de or het together.

lines.speaker: Sanne:
lines.text: Twee derde is de, één derde is het. Dus gok maar de.
lines.id: Two thirds are de, one third is het. So if you have to guess, go for de.
lines.literal: two third is de, one third is het. so guess just de.

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: In het meervoud is alles de. De tafels, de boeken.
lines.id: In the plural everything is de. De tafels, de boeken.
lines.literal: in the plural is everything de. the tables, the books.

lines.speaker: Docent:
lines.text: Precies. En één trucje: alles met -je is het. Het tafeltje.
lines.id: Exactly. And one trick: everything with -je is het. Het tafeltje.
lines.literal: exactly. and one little-trick: everything with -je is het. the little-table.

notes: **Dit is een tafel** → a sentence that introduces a thing. Once it has been introduced, it becomes "that one" and takes *de*/*het*. Exactly like English *a* → *the*.
**Daar is geen regel voor** — the preposition *voor* is thrown to the end (compare English "there's no rule *for* it"). For now, learn the shape; the pattern is explained in Units 10 and 14.

**Geen** means "no / not a" and is used to negate nouns: *geen regel* (no rule), *geen tijd* (no time). Everything else is negated with *niet*. The difference between *geen* and *niet* is covered in Unit 4 — it is one of the most common beginner mistakes.
**Twee derde … één derde** — fractions are built from the number + *-de/-ste*, just as in English (third, fifth). The full set of numbers is in Unit 6.
**In het meervoud is alles de.** This is truly great news: as soon as a noun goes plural, the *de/het* question is over. All plural nouns take *de*.
**Gok maar de** — if you really don't know, guess *de*: the odds are about two to one. A wrong guess rarely makes you unintelligible; it just sounds like an accent.

**Het tafeltje** — the ending *-je* makes a noun "small" (*verkleinwoord*, a diminutive), and **every** word ending in *-je* is a het-woord, no exceptions. This is the only de/het rule you can trust 100%.

grammars.title: Articles: een, de, het
body: Dutch has one indefinite article (*een*, a/an) and two definite articles (*de* and *het*, the) — where English gets by with a single *the*.
after: Look at the last two rows: even *this* and *that* follow the noun's group. *Deze/die* for de-woorden, *dit/dat* for het-woorden. In the plural it's always *deze/die*.
In speech, *het* often shrinks to **'t**: *'t huis*, *'t is goed*. You'll hear it constantly; writing it that way is only normal in casual writing.

⚠️ When introducing something, use *dit is* / *dat is* for **every** noun, de-woorden included: *Dit is een tafel* (not *deze is een tafel*). *Deze/die* are used when the noun follows: *deze tafel is bruin*.

grammars.title: The groups you can predict
body: There's no overall rule, but a few groups are truly reliable. Learning this short list saves you hundreds of guesses.

tables.title: Always het
head: Group
Examples
rows: het meisje, het kopje, het broodje
het eten, het roken, het leren
het gebouw, het bedrijf, het verhaal

tables.title: Always de
head: Group
Examples
rows: de leraar, de dokter, de bakker
de woning, de waarheid, de politie
de appel, de boom, de drie

after: The most famous exception: **het meisje** (girl) is a het-woord — not because Dutch considers girls to be objects, but because of *-je*. The ending rule beats everything.
In dictionaries the group is shown as *de* / *het*, or sometimes as **(m/v)** and **(o)** — *onzijdig* (neuter) means het-woord.

blocks.text: Almost every Dutch noun forms its plural with **-en** (pronounced -uh). A small group uses **-s**, just like English, and you can spot that group by the sound of the last syllable.

head: Ending
Rule
Examples
rows: the default for almost every word
after a single a, i, o, u, y
a small group of old words

blocks.title: Spelling that changes too — and why
items: *man → mannen*: the consonant is **doubled** so the vowel stays short.
*boot → boten*: the double vowel is **shortened** because the syllable is now open and the sound stays long anyway.
*huis → huizen*, *brief → brieven*: **s → z** and **f → v** between two vowels (compare English *house → houses*, *leaf → leaves*).
All these changes are about spelling, not grammar: they exist precisely to keep the sound the same.

blocks.text: Like English, Dutch **must** mark the plural, even after a number: *drie boeken*, not *drie boek*. The difference is that *-en*, not *-s*, is the default.

Learn these columns **whole, with the article**, as if it were one word: not *tafel* but *detafel*. Learning the noun first and its article later almost never works — it is the advice Dutch teachers repeat most often all over the world.

blocks.title: The small form (-je) is used far more than you'd think
items: *een biertje* = a glass of beer (ordering *een bier* sounds like you want to buy a whole barrel).
*een kopje koffie* = a cup of coffee, *een broodje* = a sandwich roll, *een uurtje* = an hour or so.
The small form softens a request: *een momentje* (just a sec), *een vraagje* (a quick question).
The form is **-je**, but it changes to **-tje**, **-pje**, **-etje** depending on the last sound: *auto → autootje*, *boom → boompje*, *bal → balletje*.
⚠️ And once more: whatever it started as, the result is always a **het**-woord.
